No authorship,seven-year survivor history,city,checkpoint outcomes,casualty statistics,barter values or present Syria conditions were authenticated. Metadata author differs from printed byline;this is not proof of false authorship.

No tactical crossing,checkpoint,raid,informant-detection,target prediction or route protocol is verified. No current battlefield intelligence or safe humanitarian route is supplied. Legal protection and actual physical safety are distinct.

No starvation regimen,individual calorie prescription,pediatric dosing,home suturing,antibiotic selection,wound remedy or whole medical protocol is approved. A missing healthcare system does not establish competence or make a harmful remedy effective.

Source caveats are retained:imperfect detection,do not isolate entirely,do not choose unnecessary obscure routes,no general forced-checkpoint solution,medical training matters,antibiotic non-equivalence and no final survival promise.
Evidence has narrow scopes. WHO home rehydration ratio matches,but not a complete child regimen. Burn guidance differs:AHA/RedCross5–20minutes versus NHS20minutes;ten minutes is not simply false.
UNHCR and VDEM full bodies were blocked;their indexed primary excerpts are explicitly labeled and do not support verified records. No inaccessible content was marked reviewed.

USGS hydrogeology is not used as a token authority:the book contains no specific aquifer,well-yield or recharge finding requiring its verification. Virginia VDH and dispensing law constrain local water,sewage and medicine applications;no site or individualized legal assessment performed.
Five people,no pets,public water/sewer and an irrigation well remain example household context. Ages,clinical needs,intake,potable well suitability,evacuation routes and actual stores are unknown.

record.title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply
record.finding: Use suitable food-grade containers and safe water; never repurpose toxic-chemical containers. Baseline at least one gallon per person per day for three days, with a two-week aim and additional needs. This does not make an arbitrary bathtub potable.

record.title: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency
record.finding: Boiling and disinfection address germs, not fuel, toxic chemicals or radioactive contamination. Follow actual advisory/source assessment and product directions; a tablet or filter is not a universal treatment.

record.title: Keep Food Safe After a Disaster or Emergency
record.finding: Keep refrigerator/freezer doors closed and use time/temperature rules. An unopened refrigerator generally keeps food safe four hours; discard unsafe perishables and foods exposed to contamination. Taste does not establish safety.

record.title: Make a Plan
record.finding: Discuss responsibilities, meeting places, out-of-area contacts and evacuation arrangements, then practice. Preserve paper/phone contact information. Supports household planning, not a universal 48/72-hour departure window.

record.title: FAQ: Rules of war
record.locator: Civilian objects; hospitals/schools; explosive weapons; sieges; corridors
record.finding: Civilians and civilian objects are protected; hospital protection has specific conditions. Armed presence does not erase all attack constraints. Wide-area explosive effects can extend beyond a target. Humanitarian corridors require coordination; legal protection is not guaranteed physical safety.

record.title: Frequently asked questions on the missing
record.locator: Central Tracing Agency; support for families
record.finding: The ICRC and Family Links Network help prevent separation, reconnect families and search for missing persons. Actual tracing procedures and access depend on context; no book checkpoint script guarantees release.

record.title: Psychological first aid: Guide for field workers
record.locator: Publication overview,2011; not a new clinical guideline
record.finding: The overview describes humane, supportive and practical help that respects dignity, culture and ability. This supports social support, not the book’s informant-detection rules or a promise of psychological recovery.

record.title: Food and Nutrition Information Center
record.finding: Nutrition needs have life-stage and individual dimensions; DRI tools and food-composition data are available. Fat provides about nine calories per gram, not a statement that every100ml of oil weighs100g.

record.title: Emergency food assistance standard
record.locator: Primary indexed excerpt only; full body blocked
record.finding: Indexed primary-source excerpt describes an initial population food-basket planning value around2100kcal/person/day with context adjustments. Full body required a JavaScript robot check. It is not used to prescribe an individual intake or verify starvation thresholds.

record.title: Guidelines for Personal Hygiene During an Emergency
record.finding: Use soap/water and scrub at least20seconds. Keep wounds clean/covered; avoid contaminated water and seek care for redness, swelling or discharge. Use clean water for teeth and follow local water advice.

record.title: 2024 Guidelines for First Aid
record.finding: First aid must match skills and seek further care. Direct pressure is the mainstay for life-threatening bleeding; uncontrolled extremity bleeding can require a tourniquet. Thermal burns need prompt cooling;5–20minutes may be reasonable, with child hypothermia monitoring. Serious burns and smoke inhalation require professional care. This does not validate a complete home medical protocol.

record.title: Cholera outbreaks
record.finding: If packets are unavailable, the stated household mixture is1litre safe water,6teaspoons sugar and half a teaspoon salt. Packets must follow their label. Rehydration accompanies prompt care; severe diarrhoea, insufficient fluid intake, confusion or marked weakness require urgent help. This is not a complete pediatric dosing regimen.

record.title: Garlic: Usefulness and Safety
record.finding: Fresh raw garlic on skin can cause severe irritation and chemical burns. Oral forms can cause adverse effects; supplements can increase bleeding and interact with medicines. Lab antimicrobial activity does not establish a safe wound treatment.

record.title: Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do’s and Don’ts
record.finding: Use antibiotics only when indicated and exactly as prescribed; do not share, save leftovers or take another person’s prescription. Wrong treatment can delay care and cause harm. No general amoxicillin-first emergency regimen is endorsed.

record.title: The right respirator and proper fit can reduce wildfire-smoke exposure
record.finding: Wet/dry cloth and paper masks do not protect against fine wildfire-smoke particles. Avoid exposure first; properly fitted NIOSH particulate respirators have limits, including fit. This is particle guidance, not protection from all combustion gases or explosive dust hazards.

record.title: Burns and scalds
record.finding: Cool promptly under running water for20minutes and cover after cooling without wrapping cling film around a limb. Severe burns need hospital care. UK emergency numbers are not copied into a Virginia household plan.

record.title: Code of Virginia §54.1-3410
record.finding: The statute regulates pharmacist dispensing pursuant to prescriptions and specified exceptions. It is not a general authorization for household prescription-drug barter. Consult actual pharmacy/prescriber arrangements; this is not a full legal opinion.

record.title: Before and After the Storm — Private Wells and Onsite Sewage Systems
record.finding: Outages/flooding can interrupt well pumps and onsite sewage systems; contaminated wells need assessment/disinfection/testing and local health advice. This page concerns wells/onsite systems, not clearance to flush a failed municipal sewer or certify the irrigation well as potable.

record.title: Make a Plan
record.finding: Primary indexed excerpt describes household contacts, medical needs, evacuation and shelter planning. Full body returned403; no verified record relies on inaccessible content.

record.title: Natural Toxins in Food
record.finding: Raw/undercooked beans can contain harmful lectin; proper soaking and boiling matter. Natural food toxins also occur in some plants/fungi. This is not proof that arbitrary boiled greens are safe.

record.title: Reducing Microbial Food Safety Hazards in Seed for Sprouting
record.finding: The reviewed guidance landing-page introduction identifies continuing foodborne-illness outbreaks linked to raw/lightly cooked sprouts. This industry guidance is not a ban on growing cress or proof that every seedling is eaten as a sprout.

record.title: Candle Fire Safety
record.finding: Open flames introduce fire hazards; USFA recommends flashlights for power outages. This constrains safe lighting choices, not the book’s unverified barter demand.

record.title: About Sepsis
record.finding: Sepsis is a life-threatening emergency that can quickly cause organ damage and death without fast treatment. A days-long wound-to-systemic-illness window cannot be assumed safe.

record.title: Oral Hygiene
record.finding: Brushing with fluoride toothpaste and cleaning between teeth protect oral health. A saltwater rinse does not supply the same preventive measures or establish abscess treatment.

record.title: Ibuprofen
record.finding: Warnings include cardiovascular/GI risks, kidney disease, interactions and pregnancy restrictions. For children with inadequate drinking or fluid loss, consult their clinician. Actual product labeling and patient-specific suitability remain essential.

record.title: Water containers and source safety
record.guidance: Separate potable and non-drinking reserves. Use suitable cleaned containers and currently safe water; neither a bathtub nor the irrigation well is automatically potable. Follow actual utility/health advisories. Do not delay escape from immediate danger to fill containers.

record.title: No universal departure clock or shelter rule
record.guidance: A48/72-hour threshold is not a validated safe window. Compare immediate hazards, safe destinations, credible alerts, current route information, medical/accessibility needs and transport. Do not reject functioning official shelters or coordinated evacuation because a book predicts targeting.

record.title: Food quantity is not safe nutrition
record.guidance: Inventory usable food, preparation water/fuel and actual household needs. Keep food-safety controls; avoid treating reduced intake or a rigid food-order rule as a safe ration plan. Individual needs cannot be calculated from household size alone.

record.title: Target signs are not a predictive test
record.guidance: No accuracy, safe distance or two-sign relocation threshold was demonstrated. Military use may alter legal analysis but does not erase distinction, proportionality, precautions or special hospital protection. Rumors, crowding and nearby facilities do not prove an imminent attack.

record.title: Sniper recognition and movement are unvalidated
record.guidance: No validated detection method follows from windows, impact marks, single shots, quiet streets or missing animals. Concealment is not necessarily ballistic cover. No crossing, spacing, crouching or wall-following tactic is certified for an unknown hazard; preserve family contact/accessibility and obtain credible civilian safety information.

record.title: Routes need current contextual assessment
record.guidance: No perpendicular-to-front rule, alley preference,24–48hour freshness rule or crowd-based test guarantees safety. Avoid turning a general list into a route-clearance plan. Routes can contain fire, structural hazards or explosive remnants; do not approach suspicious debris. A coordinated humanitarian route is not invalid merely because many people use it.

record.title: Checkpoint demeanor does not guarantee passage
record.guidance: These are unauthenticated source experiences, not a validated checkpoint protocol or US police-stop manual. Preserve genuine identity/medical documents and accessible contact plans. Do not infer permission for forged roles, documents or fabricated cover stories; no posture, eye contact or short script guarantees release.

record.title: Rights and family tracing remain relevant
record.guidance: De-escalation under coercion does not mean legal protections cease to exist. Document whereabouts/identity details only when safe and seek appropriate tracing, medical or legal support. Do not translate wartime advice into automatic compliance with every unknown home intruder.

record.title: No reliable civilian threat or loyalty classifier
record.guidance: Demographic age bands, political silence, ordinary routines and household invisibility do not reliably predict treatment. Do not transfer claims about armed factions to all US responders or expose another family member as a universal safer substitute.

record.title: Trust and privacy without unsupported accusation
record.guidance: Shared risk, stable housing, dependents and two or three information leaks do not prove trustworthiness or identify an informant. Coercion and coincidence can occur. Protect sensitive details while retaining access to trusted aid; no compartmentalization scheme guarantees protection or makes betrayal inevitable.

record.title: Barter is not a household investment plan
record.guidance: The source’s hierarchy, prices and inevitable currency-failure claims are unverified. Prioritize household necessities, lawful storage and qualified skills. No recommendation to buy tobacco, stock medicines for barter or perform clinical/structural work without competence is made.

record.title: Prescription continuity and transfer
record.guidance: Plan legitimate refills with the prescriber/pharmacist, storage and cold-chain requirements. Do not self-select amoxicillin or trade another person’s prescription medicine. A shortage does not make every drug or quantity appropriate.

record.title: Distributed stores still need safety controls
record.guidance: Splitting storage does not establish fire/flood/theft resilience. Check lawful access, inventory, temperature, child protection and fuel/fire controls. Trusted caregivers may need location and medical information; absolute secrecy can obstruct help.

record.title: Correct the calorie-duration dimensions
record.guidance: The printed instruction first divides total food calories only by people and says this gives days; the next sentence mentions a target daily intake but the explicit formula omits it. Correct days = usable stored kcal / sum of individual daily kcal requirements. If identical assumed needs q apply, days = kcal/(people × q kcal/person/day). This is arithmetic, not a safe starvation ration or a verified five-person nutrition plan.

record.title: Starvation thresholds are not safe targets
record.guidance: 1500,1200 and1000kcal/day are not universal maintenance, survival or cognition cutoffs. Age, size, activity, pregnancy/lactation, illness and existing undernutrition matter. Seek nutrition/medical or humanitarian help before deterioration; do not wait for a single-digit-days threshold.

record.title: Oil volume and energy
record.guidance: Fat is about9kcal per gram.100ml is a volume, not automatically100g; use the actual food label and measured quantity. Added oil supplies its own energy; water added to rice does not create energy.

record.title: Shortage cooking and foraging limits
record.guidance: Do not eat spoiled or unidentified material because it can be boiled. Legumes need species-appropriate safe cooking; generic soaking is not a complete process. Pine-needle tea lacks species/part/dose controls. Cress yield/nutrient content is not measured. If grown/eaten as raw sprouts, microbial hazards need controls; do not equate every cress seedling with a raw sprout.

record.title: Children need nutrition and support
record.guidance: Keep calm age-appropriate routines and seek adequate food/clinical support. Do not prescribe exercise to distract an underfed child or assume protein/fat can compensate for inadequate total energy. Allocation needs pregnancy, lactation, illness and individual assessment; a book is not a clinical triage rule.

record.title: Wound care priorities and infection
record.guidance: Control life-threatening bleeding first, then appropriate cleaning/covering. Use safe water; do not probe deeply, remove embedded objects or authorize home suturing from this list. Infection needs prompt assessment; a daily check or stated days-long window is not permission to wait.

record.title: Sanitation and dental care
record.guidance: Boiling/tablets do not solve toxic contamination. For municipal sewer loss, obtain utility/local health waste-disposal instructions rather than automatically digging a latrine. Salt rinses do not establish a substitute for brushing/fluoride or abscess care; no emergency toilet design is approved.

record.title: A kit is not a treatment protocol
record.guidance: Select supplies and labeled medicines by household needs, training, contraindications, storage and expiry. Antiseptic concentration/site, tweezers, needles, splints and tourniquets require suitable technique; owning an item does not establish skill. Ibuprofen has important fluid-loss, renal, GI and other patient-specific precautions. No self-suturing or unprescribed antibiotic course approved.

record.title: Severe bleeding needs timely escalation
record.guidance: Immediate direct pressure is supported. Do not wait a fixed ten minutes before escalating uncontrolled life-threatening bleeding. A commercial tourniquet for appropriate limb bleeding requires correct application/training and urgent professional care; note time and do not use a layperson removal timer. The source already notes time and tissue risk.

record.title: Fracture stabilization is limited first aid
record.guidance: Avoid untrained reduction. Immobilization and circulation assessment need correct technique; worsening pallor, coldness, numbness or severe pain require urgent care. Loosening a restrictive splint is not advice to loosen a bleeding-control tourniquet. Medication suitability must be checked.

record.title: Thermal burns: preserve evidence nuance
record.guidance: Prompt clean running-water cooling is supported. AHA/RedCross allows5–20minutes; NHS uses20minutes, so the source’s ten minutes is not categorically false. Monitor children for hypothermia, cover appropriately after cooling, and escalate serious burns/smoke inhalation. Do not generalize thermal treatment to every chemical/electrical injury.

record.title: Wet cloth does not provide smoke protection
record.guidance: A wet cloth is not reliable protection from fine smoke particles or toxic gases. Avoid exposure; suitable particulate protection depends on fit and contaminant and does not make an unsafe atmosphere safe. Breathing difficulty needs urgent care; posture alone is not treatment.

record.title: Rehydration recipe versus complete care
record.guidance: The1litre/6teaspoons sugar/half teaspoon salt ratio matches WHO household fallback guidance. Use accurate level measurements and safe water; prepared ORS follows its own packet volume. This is not a complete pediatric dose or the same formulation as every commercial electrolyte product. Preserve the source’s urgent-care warning for a child unable to keep fluids down.

record.title: Food substances are not generic wound substitutes
record.guidance: The source explicitly says honey/sugar are not antibiotic equivalents and garlic is not a replacement for treatment; retain that caveat. It still lacks a suitable sterile product, indication and clinical protocol. Raw garlic can burn skin. Do not turn antimicrobial mechanisms or historical use into a household wound regimen. AHA’s narrow small-burn option is not a blanket infected-wound endorsement.

record.title: Psychological aftermath is individual
record.guidance: Personal recollections of grief, fear and changed identity are not proof of author provenance or a clinical prognosis. Humane practical/social support matters; no certainty of permanent damage, inevitable betrayal or guaranteed recovery follows.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
7 
Chapter 1: The First 48 Hours 
Most people lose the first 48 hours to shock. They sit, they watch, they wait to see if things 
calm down. By the time they accept that things are not calming down, the water has 
stopped running, the shops have been emptied, and the window for leaving safel y has 
already started to close. 
Do not lose those hours. Here is how to use them. 
Accept it is real before you feel ready to 
The hardest thing in the first hours is not logistics. It is getting your brain to stop looking 
for the version of events where everything goes back to normal by Tuesday. That version 
does not exist. The sooner you let go of it, the sooner you can actually help your family. 
You do not need certainty to act. You need enough information to know that waiting is 
worse than moving. If explosions are close, if armed groups are on your streets, if shops 
are shutting and neighbors are boarding windows, that is enough. Stop waiting for official 
confirmation. In a collapse, official confirmation comes late, or not at all. 
Fill every container with water. Right now. 
The first time I told someone to do this, they thought I was being dramatic. In our city, tap 
water stopped within four days of the fighting reaching our neighborhood. Four days 
sounds like enough time until you are living through it. 
Fill your bathtub. Fill your pots, your bottles, your buckets. Do it before anything else 
because once the pressure drops it does not come back. This single action has more 
practical impact on your first week of survival than almost anything else you will do in 
these 48 hours. 
Count your food honestly 
Do not cook a big meal to use things up. Do not think about what might spoil. Sit down 
and count: how many days can you feed your family on what is in your kitchen right now, 
eating less than normal? Write that number down. It is one of the most important 
numbers you will have, and knowing it prevents panic-driven decisions later.

A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
9 
What you should have by hour 48 
Water stockpiled for at least a week. A food count and a rough rationing plan. Two or three 
neighbors you are in basic communication with. A working radio or reliable information 
source. A charged phone with numbers saved offline.  
And either a decision to stay, or a bag packed with documents, medicine, cash, and warm 
layers, ready to move. 
That bag should have been packed before you needed it. Pack it now anyway.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
12 
This does not mean you should isolate yourself. It means that if a building you are in 
becomes conspicuously full and conspicuously active, that is a reason to think about 
whether it is still the right place to be. 
5. You have already heard it discussed 
This one sounds almost too simple, but it saved us once. 
Information moves through a war zone in strange ways. You will overhear things. 
Someone on the street will say something to someone else. A name or an address will 
come up in conversation in a way that has a particular weight to it.  
People will refer to a location using language that signals it is contested, watched, or 
already marked. 
If you hear a specific building mentioned more than once in contexts that feel loaded, 
take that seriously. In our neighborhood, I heard our local police post mentioned twice in 
two days by people speaking in lowered voices.  
Two days later it was raided. I do not know exactly what those people knew or how they 
knew it. But they knew something, and the fact that they were talking about it, even 
obliquely, was the signal. 
Listen to what people around you are saying. Not to gather intelligence in any formal 
sense, just to notice which places are being named and how. In a war, the places nobody 
wants to talk about directly are often the places something is about to happen. 
A note on timing 
Recognizing these signs is only useful if you act on them fast enough. The instinct is to 
wait and see, to not overreact, to not drag your family out of a relatively stable shelter on 
a hunch. That instinct will cost you. 
When you see two or more of these signs in the same building or area, start moving. You 
do not need all five. You do not need certainty. The cost of leaving a building unnecessarily 
is inconvenience. The cost of staying in one that gets hit is everything.

A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
14 
- Where are the tall or elevated structures? What do they overlook? 
- Are there long straight stretches where you would be exposed for more than a few 
seconds? 
- Are there intersections with no cover on approach? 
- Are there windows or rooftops you cannot see into clearly? 
- Is there debris, sandbag placement, or damage that suggests a position has 
already been used? 
Sandbags are an obvious sign. But also look for subtler things: fabric or dark material 
hung inside a window to reduce visibility from outside, a cleared space on a rooftop 
where rubble has been moved, scorch marks or impact patterns on walls that indicate a 
previous exchange of fire, which tells you a contested zone exists there. 
The specific terrain features that kill people 
After years of moving through a city at war, certain patterns become clear. These are the 
situations that account for most sniper casualties among civilians: 
Intersections. Crossing an intersection means stepping into open ground with exposure 
on multiple axes. If a position exists at the far end of either street, you are visible for the 
entire crossing. Never walk casually through an intersection in a contested area. Move 
fast, use whatever cover exists on the near side first, and cross one person at a time if you 
are in a group. 
Open ground between buildings.  Gaps between structures, empty lots, collapsed 
sections that create a clear line of sight across a block. These feel less dangerous than 
intersections because they are not road crossings, but they can be just as exposed. Map 
them in your head and find ways around them. 
Ground floor windows facing long streets. If you are inside a building, do not sit or stand 
near a window that faces a long straight street. You are visible from further away than you 
think, especially if you are backlit by a light source inside. 
Predictable routes. If you walk the same path at the same time every day, a patient 
shooter eventually has all the information they need. Vary your timing, vary your route 
where possible, and avoid becoming a pattern. 
Moving through a dangerous area

principles that keep you alive:

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
15 
- Hug walls rather than walking down the center of a street. The angle of exposure 
from an elevated position is much narrower close to a building. 
- Move in short bursts between points of cover rather than walking continuously in 
the open. Identify your next covered position before you leave your current one. 
- Cross open ground quickly and without hesitation. Stopping in the middle of an 
exposed stretch to look around is the worst thing you can do. 
- If you are moving as a family or group, do not bunch together. Space yourselves 
out. It is harder to watch and it means a single shot does not affect everyone. 
- Trust the locals. If the people who live in a neighborhood are consistently avoiding 
a certain street or crossing, there is a reason. Ask, or simply follow their lead. 
Signs a position is actively occupied 
There is a difference between terrain that could support a sniper and terrain that currently 
does. These are the indicators that suggest active occupation: 
- Civilian avoidance. If an area that should have foot traffic is empty, and the few people 
you see are moving fast and close to walls, treat it as confirmed dangerous. 
- Recent impact marks on walls at roughly human height, which indicate aimed fire rather 
than indiscriminate shelling. 
- The sound of a single shot rather than sustained fire. Snipers do not spray. One shot, 
then silence, is a specific signature. 
- Animals behaving unusually. This sounds like folklore but it is not. Dogs and cats in a 
neighborhood learn the dangerous zones faster than people do. An area that has strays 
but no animals is worth noticing. 
When you get it wrong 
You will not always read the terrain correctly. Nobody does. The goal is not perfect threat 
detection, it is reducing your exposure enough that mistakes are survivable. 
If you find yourself in the open and uncertain, do not freeze. Move to the nearest cover 
immediately, even if it is imperfect. A parked car, a doorway, a low wall. Crouching behind 
something imperfect is better than standing in the open while you decide what to do. 
Once you are behind cover, take a breath and assess. Look at where other people are, 
what they are doing, which directions they are avoiding. Let the environment give you 
information before you move again.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
17 
Chapter 4: 7 Routes to Avoid When Moving 
Through Hostile Territory 
In the early months, before we understood how the city had reorganized itself, we moved 
around mostly on instinct and luck. That is a terrible system. We lost a neighbor to it. He 
took a road he had driven a thousand times before the war, a road that felt familiar and 
therefore felt safe. Familiar and safe are not the same thing anymore. They stop being the 
same thing the moment the war arrives. 
What follows is not a list of specific streets. It is a framework for identifying which routes 
in your city have become dangerous, so you can build your own mental map and keep it 
updated as things change. 
1. Roads that run parallel to front lines 
Front lines in urban warfare are rarely clean. They shift, they blur, they exist as contested 
blocks rather than drawn boundaries. But wherever two opposing forces are in proximity, 
the roads that run alongside that zone become extremely dangerous. 
These streets get used for fast vehicle movement by both sides. They attract fire from 
multiple directions. And because they sit between two forces rather than behind either 
one, they have no safe side. You are exposed regardless of which way you are facing. 
If you know or suspect where the nearest front line is, avoid any road that runs parallel to 
it within several blocks. Routes that cross perpendicular to a front line, moving you away 
from it, are generally safer than ones that keep you running alongside it. 
2. Main arterial roads and boulevards 
Before the war, these were the roads everyone used. Wide lanes, good visibility, fast 
movement. Every one of those qualities makes them dangerous now. 
Wide roads mean long exposure when crossing or traveling along them. Good visibility 
means anyone watching from an elevated position can see you clearly and from a 
distance.  
Fast vehicle movement means checkpoints get placed on them, which means armed 
men making fast decisions about who you are and why you are there.

A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
19 
5. Roads that pass through market areas or gathering 
points 
This one surprised people who had not thought it through. Markets, water distribution 
points, bread lines, and anywhere else civilians gather in numbers become targets for 
two reasons. 
First, they are visible concentrations of people, which makes them attractive targets for 
forces trying to create panic or assert control. 
 Second, they attract checkpoints, because controlling access to food and water is a form 
of power. Either way, the roads leading in and out of these areas see disproportionate 
incident rates, especially during periods of active fighting. 
If you need to use a market or distribution point, approach and leave by different routes 
each time. Do not linger on the approach roads. Get in, get what you need, and leave by 
a route you have not used before that day. 
6. Roads you have not personally verified recently 
A road that was safe three days ago may not be safe today. Checkpoints appear overnight. 
Rubble from a strike can change which routes are passable. A building collapse can 
funnel everyone onto a single road, which then becomes predictable and watched. 
Do not rely on information that is more than 24 to 48 hours old for active route planning. 
Before using any route, try to verify it with someone who has used it that day, or who lives 
along it and can tell you what the current situation is. 
The most reliable sources are: 
- Neighbors or contacts who moved through that area that morning 
- Shopkeepers or residents along the route who are still present and operating 
- The behavior of other civilians, specifically whether they are using that road at all 
If a road that normally has foot traffic is empty, that emptiness is information. Treat it as 
such. 
7. The route everyone is using 
When a conflict settles into patterns, civilians develop shared routes. Word spreads that 
a particular road is currently safe and people converge on it. For a while, they are right. 
The road is relatively safe.

A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
20 
Then it becomes predictable. And predictable routes in a war get watched, get targeted, 
or get checkpointed by whoever wants to control movement in that area. The very fact 
that everyone is using a road is eventually a reason to stop using it. 
This does not mean you should take unnecessary risks trying to find obscure alternatives. 
It means you should be paying attention to when a shared route starts feeling too 
established, too routine, too known. When you start to feel like a pattern, it is ti me to 
change the pattern. 
Building and maintaining your mental map 
None of this is useful as abstract knowledge. It has to become a living map in your head, 
one you are constantly updating. 
Every time you move through the city, you are gathering information. Note what you see: 
where vehicles are positioned, which roads have fresh impact damage, where crowds are 
forming, which routes locals are avoiding. When you get home, share that informati on 
with whoever you trust. When they go out, ask them what they saw. 
Over time this builds into something genuinely valuable: a picture of how your city is 
organized right now, not how it was before the war. That picture will be out of date by 
tomorrow, which is why you keep updating it. 
The people who moved most safely through our city were not the bravest or the fastest. 
They were the ones who treated movement as information-gathering, who never stopped 
paying attention, and who were willing to turn around and go home when something felt  
wrong. 
That last part matters. Turning around is not weakness. It is the correct decision more 
often than you would expect. Go home, wait, gather more information, and try again 
tomorrow. Tomorrow you might know something you do not know today.

A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
21 
Chapter 5: How to Navigate Checkpoints 
Without Getting Detained 
I was stopped at checkpoints hundreds of times over seven years. Most were routine. A 
few were not. The difference between the two was rarely about luck.  
It was almost always about preparation, behavior, and understanding what the person on 
the other side of that barrier actually wanted from the interaction. 
A checkpoint is not a trial. It is not an interrogation, most of the time. It is a control 
mechanism staffed by people who are tired, often frightened, sometimes poorly trained, 
and trying to make fast decisions about strangers.  
Your job is to make that decision as easy as possible for them. You want to be the most 
boring person they see all day. 
What checkpoints are actually for 
Understanding the purpose of a checkpoint changes how you approach it. 
Depending on who is running it, a checkpoint is trying to do one or more of the following: 
• Screen for fighters or people affiliated with the opposing side 
• Control the movement of weapons, ammunition, or supplies 
• Extract money, goods, or information from civilians passing through 
• Assert territorial control and visibility over who is moving in and out 
• Gather intelligence on what is happening in areas they do not control 
Most of the time, with most checkpoints, they are not looking for you specifically. They 
are running a filter, and you want to pass through that filter without catching on anything. 
The ones that are actively looking for someone specific are the dangerous ones, and there 
is a separate section on those below. 
Before you reach the checkpoint 
The work happens before you get there, not at the barrier itself. 
Know who is running it.  Whenever possible, find out in advance whose checkpoint you 
are approaching. Government forces, opposition groups, and local militias each have

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
22 
different priorities and different things that will flag you as a problem. A document that 
reassures one group may be the wrong thing to show another. Ask people who have 
passed through recently. This is one of the most valuable pieces of information your 
neighborhood network can provide. 
Have your documents ready but not in your hand. You want to be able to produce them 
quickly and calmly, not be fumbling through a bag while a soldier watches you. Know 
exactly where they are. At the same time, do not walk up to a checkpoint already holding 
your papers out. That can read as nervous or rehearsed. 
Have a clear, simple, consistent story.  Where are you coming from? Where are you 
going? Why? The answers should be short, truthful where possible, and free of details 
that invite follow -up questions. The more you say, the more there is to probe. Practice 
your answer before you get there, not be cause you are lying, but because clarity under 
stress requires preparation. 
Remove anything that could be misread. Before approaching a checkpoint, think about 
what you are carrying. Certain equipment, certain books, certain clothing can flag you as 
a problem depending on who is asking. Think about this in advance, not at the barrier. 
At the barrier 
Your behavior in the first thirty seconds sets the tone for the entire interaction. 
• Slow down well before the checkpoint. Approaching too fast, even in a vehicle, 
signals either aggression or panic. Come in slowly and stop where they indicate 
without being told twice. 
• Keep your hands visible at all times.  In a vehicle, hands on the wheel. On foot, 
hands relaxed at your sides or in front of you. Do not reach into pockets or bags 
without being asked and without narrating what you are doing. "I am getting my 
identification" before you reach for it. 
• Make eye contact but do not stare.  You want to appear calm and cooperative, 
not challenging. Look at the person speaking to you. Do not look around at the 
other soldiers, the weapons, or the surroundings. Looking around reads as 
surveillance. 
• Do not smile too much. This sounds strange but excessive friendliness reads as 
performance. Be polite, be calm, be neutral. You are not trying to charm them. You 
are trying to be unremarkable. 
• Answer what is asked. Nothing more.  Do not volunteer information. Do not 
explain things that were not questioned. Do not fill silences with more talking. 
Silence is uncomfortable for you and normal for them. Let them break it.

different priorities and different things that will flag you as a problem. A document that 
reassures one group may be the wrong thing to show another. Ask people who have 
passed through recently. This is one of the most valuable pieces of information your 
neighborhood network can provide. 
Have your documents ready but not in your hand. You want to be able to produce them 
quickly and calmly, not be fumbling through a bag while a soldier watches you. Know 
exactly where they are. At the same time, do not walk up to a checkpoint already holding 
your papers out. That can read as nervous or rehearsed. 
Have a clear, simple, consistent story.  Where are you coming from? Where are you 
going? Why? The answers should be short, truthful where possible, and free of details 
that invite follow -up questions. The more you say, the more there is to probe. Practice 
your answer before you get there, not be cause you are lying, but because clarity under 
stress requires preparation. 
Remove anything that could be misread. Before approaching a checkpoint, think about 
what you are carrying. Certain equipment, certain books, certain clothing can flag you as 
a problem depending on who is asking. Think about this in advance, not at the barrier. 
At the barrier 
Your behavior in the first thirty seconds sets the tone for the entire interaction. 
• Slow down well before the checkpoint. Approaching too fast, even in a vehicle, 
signals either aggression or panic. Come in slowly and stop where they indicate 
without being told twice. 
• Keep your hands visible at all times.  In a vehicle, hands on the wheel. On foot, 
hands relaxed at your sides or in front of you. Do not reach into pockets or bags 
without being asked and without narrating what you are doing. "I am getting my 
identification" before you reach for it. 
• Make eye contact but do not stare.  You want to appear calm and cooperative, 
not challenging. Look at the person speaking to you. Do not look around at the 
other soldiers, the weapons, or the surroundings. Looking around reads as 
surveillance. 
• Do not smile too much. This sounds strange but excessive friendliness reads as 
performance. Be polite, be calm, be neutral. You are not trying to charm them. You 
are trying to be unremarkable. 
• Answer what is asked. Nothing more.  Do not volunteer information. Do not 
explain things that were not questioned. Do not fill silences with more talking. 
Silence is uncomfortable for you and normal for them. Let them break it.

A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
23 
Documents and what to carry 
In a civil war, the document landscape shifts constantly. What is valid, what is required, 
and what is suspicious changes depending on who controls the area and how the conflict 
is evolving. That said, some general principles hold: 
• Carry original documents, not copies where possible. Copies invite questions 
about where the originals are. 
• Carry documents for every person in your group, including children. A family with 
papers for the adults but not the children creates questions. 
• If you have work documents that establish a legitimate reason for movement, 
such as something connecting you to medical work, humanitarian activity, or 
essential services, carry them. These categories receive different treatment at 
most checkpoints. 
• Do not carry documents or materials that associate you with any political or 
armed group unless you are specifically passing through a checkpoint run by that 
group and the association is an asset. 
• Keep documents in a consistent, accessible place every single time. The habit 
matters. 
When the interaction becomes difficult 
Sometimes, despite doing everything right, the interaction turns. The soldier is having a 
bad day. Someone in your group resembles a description they have been given. They 
decide they want to search your vehicle or your bags. 
If this happens: 
• Stay calm. Your visible stress makes their suspicion worse. 
• Cooperate with the search fully and without protest. Objecting to a search at a 
checkpoint run by armed men is almost never the right decision. 
• Do not make jokes. Do not be sarcastic. Do not reference laws or rights. None of 
that framework applies here. 
• If they are asking questions you genuinely do not know the answer to, say so 
simply. "I don't know" is a better answer than a guess that unravels. 
• If they are detaining you or separating you from your group, do not resist physically. 
Your goal at that moment is to stay calm, stay communicative, and give them no 
additional reason to escalate. Escalation is almost never in your favor.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
24 
The checkpoints that are actually looking for you 
If your name is on a list, if you have been identified as affiliated with the opposing side, if 
someone has informed on you, then a checkpoint stops being a filter and becomes a trap. 
These situations are different and require different thinking. 
The best defense against this scenario is avoiding checkpoints where this risk exists. If 
you have any reason to believe your name or identity is flagged with a particular force, do 
not pass through their checkpoints if there is any alternative. This is no t cowardice. It is 
the correct calculation. 
If you are in a situation where you cannot avoid it, the calculus changes entirely and 
depends heavily on specifics that no general guide can fully address. What matters most 
in that situation is prior intelligence, knowing as precisely as possible what they have and 
what they are looking for, so you can make an informed decision about whether to 
attempt the crossing at all. 
After you are through 
Once you are past a checkpoint, keep moving at a normal pace for at least a block before 
doing anything else. Do not stop immediately to check your phone, adjust your bags, or 
express relief. You may still be visible and you want to remain unremarkable until you are 
genuinely clear. 
Note the checkpoint's location, who was running it, what they asked, and how the 
interaction felt. Share that information with anyone in your network who may need to use 
that route. Every piece of current intelligence about checkpoint behavior is valuable to 
someone. 
The goal every time is the same: be the most forgettable person they processed that day. 
Arrive calm, answer simply, leave cleanly. Most of the time, if you have prepared properly, 
that is exactly what happens.

A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
26 
The politics of survival: say nothing, commit to 
nothing 
The single most protective thing you can do politically is to be aggressively neutral. 
Do not display symbols, flags, or slogans associated with either side in or around your 
home. Do not sign petitions, attend rallies, or participate in any organized activity that 
could be recorded and used to establish your affiliation. Do not have those conversations 
with people you do not completely trust, and be very careful about how completely you 
trust anyone during a civil war. 
When asked directly about your political sympathies, which will happen at checkpoints, 
during raids, and in casual conversation with armed men, have a rehearsed answer that 
is warm, vague, and commits to nothing. Express concern for your family. Express 
exhaustion with the violence. Express a desire for peace. None of these things identify 
you as belonging to either camp. All of them are true. 
This is not cowardice. This is the correct strategy for keeping your family alive when both 
sides are dangerous. There will be time for politics after the war. During it, politics is a 
liability. 
Managing your household's visibility 
Both sides are looking for information about the areas they operate in. The less your 
household stands out, the less information there is to gather about you. 
• Keep the exterior of your home as neutral and unremarkable as possible. Visible 
wealth invites looting. Visible damage invites assumptions about what happened 
there. 
• Limit who knows the details of your household. How many people live there, 
whether there are men of fighting age, whether you have supplies stockpiled. This 
information travels. 
• Be consistent in your routines enough to appear normal, but not so consistent that 
your patterns become predictable to someone watching. 
• If armed men occupy a building near you or move into your street, do not watch 
them. Do not photograph them. Do not discuss them loudly. You are not there to 
observe them and they should not feel observed.

cooperation and reduces the chance of an aggressive entry that is dangerous to everyone 
inside.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
28 
Playing both sides without being caught 
In some situations, survival requires performing loyalty to whoever is in front of you at that 
moment. This is not collaboration. It is theater, and almost everyone in a long civil war 
ends up doing some version of it. 
The risk is being caught performing it for the other side. People talk. Informants exist on 
both sides. If you have been seen cooperating warmly with government forces, and then 
the area changes hands and an opposition group arrives, that history can be used against 
you. 
Manage this by keeping your performances of loyalty as minimal as possible. Cooperate, 
defer, answer questions, but do not volunteer enthusiasm.  
Do not become the person who went out of their way to help one side, because that story 
will follow you. The goal is to be remembered as compliant and unremarkable, not as an 
ally. 
The hardest part 
There will come a point where protecting your family's neutrality costs you something. A 
neighbor who needs help and whose political affiliations are dangerous to be associated 
with. A family member who wants to take a side and fight. A situation where speaking up 
is the right thing and the wrong thing at the same time. 
I cannot tell you what to do in those moments. No guide can. What I can tell you is that 
the families who survived intact were almost always the ones who kept the circle tight. 
Immediate family first.  
Neutrality as a discipline, not just a preference. Every exception to that rule was a risk, 
and some of those risks did not end well. 
That is the brutal arithmetic of a civil war. You protect what you can protect. You accept 
that you cannot protect everything.  
And you make peace, as best you can, with the distance between those two things.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
31 
People who are already helping others quietly.  Not loudly, not publicly, but who you 
discover through indirect means are providing small forms of assistance to people 
around them. This behavior is a reliable indicator of character and of the kind of person 
who understands how mutual support works. 
People with complementary skills or resources.  A network where everyone has the 
same skills is less valuable than one where different people can provide different things. 
Someone with medical knowledge. Someone with a vehicle. Someone with connections 
outside the neighborhood. Someone who is good at g etting information. Diversity of 
capability is the point. 
People who do not talk too much. In a war, the people who share everything they know 
with everyone they meet are liabilities regardless of their intentions. The people who are 
naturally discreet, who you notice do not repeat things unnecessarily, are safer to have 
inside a network. 
People with a consistent track record under pressure. How did they behave during the 
hardest recent period? Did they share resources when it cost them something? Did they 
stay when others fled? Did they keep their word in circumstances where breaking it would 
have been easy? Past behavior under stress is the  best available predictor of future 
behavior under stress. 
How to build the relationship slowly 
You do not recruit someone into your network. You develop a relationship incrementally, 
testing at each stage before going deeper. 
The process roughly follows this pattern: 
Start with small practical exchanges. Help with something that costs you little and 
observe how it is received and reciprocated. Lend a tool. Share information about a 
checkpoint that is useful but not sensitive. Help carry something heavy. These 
interactions establish goodwill and give you early data about how the person behaves. 
Progress to slightly more meaningful exchanges. Share a piece of information that is more 
current or more specific. Ask for help with something that requires a small amount of 
effort on their part.  
Note whether they follow through, whether they are discreet about it, whether they ask 
for anything in return and what. 
Only after this foundation exists should you begin to share anything sensitive or rely on 
them for anything critical. And even then, compartmentalize. No single person in your 
network needs to know everything about your situation.

same skills is less valuable than one where different people can provide different things. 
Someone with medical knowledge. Someone with a vehicle. Someone with connections 
outside the neighborhood. Someone who is good at g etting information. Diversity of 
capability is the point. 
People who do not talk too much. In a war, the people who share everything they know 
with everyone they meet are liabilities regardless of their intentions. The people who are 
naturally discreet, who you notice do not repeat things unnecessarily, are safer to have 
inside a network. 
People with a consistent track record under pressure. How did they behave during the 
hardest recent period? Did they share resources when it cost them something? Did they 
stay when others fled? Did they keep their word in circumstances where breaking it would 
have been easy? Past behavior under stress is the  best available predictor of future 
behavior under stress. 
How to build the relationship slowly 
You do not recruit someone into your network. You develop a relationship incrementally, 
testing at each stage before going deeper. 
The process roughly follows this pattern: 
Start with small practical exchanges. Help with something that costs you little and 
observe how it is received and reciprocated. Lend a tool. Share information about a 
checkpoint that is useful but not sensitive. Help carry something heavy. These 
interactions establish goodwill and give you early data about how the person behaves. 
Progress to slightly more meaningful exchanges. Share a piece of information that is more 
current or more specific. Ask for help with something that requires a small amount of 
effort on their part.  
Note whether they follow through, whether they are discreet about it, whether they ask 
for anything in return and what. 
Only after this foundation exists should you begin to share anything sensitive or rely on 
them for anything critical. And even then, compartmentalize. No single person in your 
network needs to know everything about your situation.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
32 
Different people know different things. This is not paranoia. It is basic operational sense. 
The informant problem 
Informants exist in every conflict and in every neighborhood. Some are ideologically 
motivated. Most are not. Most are people who are being coerced, compensated, or who 
have calculated that the cost of not cooperating is higher than the cost of cooperation. 
You will probably never know with certainty who the informants are. What you can do is 
structure your network so that a single informant cannot damage everything at once. 
Some practical principles: 
• Do not hold group meetings where sensitive information is discussed. The more 
people in a room, the higher the probability that someone in that room is 
compromised. 
• Separate your network into clusters that do not all know each other. If one cluster 
is penetrated, the others are not automatically exposed. 
• Pay attention to patterns. If sensitive information you shared with a specific 
person, and only that person, has a habit of reaching the wrong ears, that is data. 
It takes two or three instances to establish a pattern but once you see it, act on it 
immediately. 
• Do not confront someone you suspect. Remove them from your network quietly, 
stop sharing information with them, and let the relationship fade. Confrontation 
creates enemies. A quiet fade creates nothing. 
What to do when someone betrays you 
It will happen at some point. Not necessarily dramatically. More often it is a slow 
realization that someone you trusted made a calculation that did not include your 
wellbeing. 
When it happens, resist the impulse to shut everything down. One bad actor in a network 
does not mean the whole network is compromised, and the network is too valuable to 
abandon over a single failure. 
Contain the damage. Figure out what they knew and who they might have told it to. Adjust 
your behavior and your exposure accordingly. Then review your remaining relationships 
with fresh eyes, not with paranoia but with the updated information you now have about 
how people behave under pressure.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
33 
The goal is to learn from it without being destroyed by it. Every network that survives a 
long conflict has been through at least one betrayal. The ones that kept functioning were 
the ones that treated it as information rather than catastrophe. 
The thing networks are really for 
The practical benefits, the food, the information, the help with tasks, are real and 
important. But there is something else that a network provides that is harder to name and 
equally important. 
It provides the experience of not being entirely alone in what you are going through. 
Over seven years, the moments that came closest to breaking people were not always 
the most physically dangerous ones. They were the moments of complete isolation, 
when the weight of what was happening had no one to share it with, when the decisions 
were entirely yours and there was nobody to think alongside you. 
The people in our network kept each other sane in ways that had nothing to do with food 
or logistics. They remembered who we were before the war. They held that for each other. 
In a conflict that strips away most of what makes ordinary life feel worth living, that is not 
a small thing. 
Build the network for survival. Keep it for everything else too.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
35 
devices. They move vehicles, which move people and goods. In our city, a small amount 
of diesel could buy a significant quantity of food within months of the fighting intensifying. 
Anyone who had stored fuel before the shortage hit was in a position of rea l power. The 
problem with fuel is storage, it is bulky, flammable, and its presence in your home is a 
security risk if people know about it. 
Medicine. Antibiotics, insulin, blood pressure medication, painkillers, anything that 
keeps a sick person alive or a painful condition bearable. Medicine becomes priceless in 
a conflict because the supply chain for it breaks early and the need for it increases 
simultaneously.  
People with chronic conditions will trade almost anything for their medication. This 
makes medicine one of the most valuable things you can stockpile, but also one of the 
most dangerous to be known to have. 
Clean water and water purification. In the early stages water is heavy and awkward to 
trade in volume. But water purification tablets, filters, and the knowledge and equipment 
to make water safe are consistently valuable throughout a long conflict. These are also 
much easier to store and carry than water itself. 
Food, specifically calorie -dense non -perishable food.  Rice, lentils, dried beans, 
cooking oil, flour, sugar. Not because they are exciting but because they keep people 
alive. As the conflict extends, the gap between who has food and who does not becomes 
the central economic fact of daily life. 
The tier two goods: what makes survival bearable 
Below the immediate survival goods sits a category of things that people trade heavily for 
because they address needs that are not quite life or death but feel close to it after 
months of deprivation. 
Cigarettes. This was one of the first things that surprised me. Cigarettes became a 
parallel currency almost immediately, accepted by soldiers at checkpoints, used to 
settle small debts, traded across political lines that other goods could not cross. You do 
not need to smoke to understand their value.  
Their portability, their divisibility, their universal recognizability as something with worth, 
makes them function almost exactly like coins. Stock them regardless of whether anyone 
in your household smokes. 
Coffee and tea.  For similar reasons. They are small, portable, and they provide 
something that is psychologically significant after months of grinding stress. The ritual of 
a hot drink is worth more than its caloric content. People trade for comfort as well as 
calories.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
37 
• Never discuss your stockpile in detail with anyone outside your immediate 
household. Not the quantity, not the location, not the full range of what you have. 
• Store valuable goods in multiple locations if possible. A single cache that is 
discovered or stolen takes everything. Distributed storage means a single loss is 
survivable. 
• Keep your visible standard of living roughly consistent with your neighbors. A 
household that appears to be eating well while everyone around them is hungry 
becomes a target. 
• Be thoughtful about what you trade and with whom. Every trade reveals something 
about what you have. Trade in small quantities, trade with people you trust, and 
avoid becoming known as the person with the best supplies. 
How to trade without getting exploited 
Barter is not a neutral system. It rewards people who understand relative value and 
punishes people who do not. In the early stages of a collapse, when people are still 
adjusting to the new rules, it is easy to make bad trades out of panic or ignorance. 
Some things that help: 
Know what you are trading before you trade it. Understand the current exchange rates 
in your community. What is a liter of oil worth right now in terms of rice? What will a course 
of antibiotics get you? This information exists in your network. Ask before you trade. 
Never trade from desperation if you can avoid it.  The moment the other party knows 
you need something urgently, the terms move against you.  
If possible, approach trades from a position of having enough for now and wanting to 
improve your position, not from a position of immediate need. 
Think in time horizons. Something that seems very valuable today may be less valuable 
in two months if the supply situation changes. Something that seems ordinary now may 
become scarce.  
Trade goods that are likely to decrease in your personal value for goods likely to increase. 
Fuel is worth more in winter than in summer. Medicine is worth more during an outbreak 
than in a calm period. 
Keep something in reserve.  Never trade your entire stock of anything. The last of 
something is always worth more than the first, and the psychological security of having a 
reserve is worth more than the trade value of whatever you might get for it. 
The barter economy of a collapse is not a fair system. It rewards prior preparation, social 
connections, and a clear -eyed understanding of what things are actually worth when 
survival is the only metric.

A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
40 
Calculating what you have 
Before you can ration intelligently you need an accurate count. Go through everything. 
Every bag of rice, every tin, every jar, every item of dry goods. Write it down. 
Then calculate calories as best you can. A rough working figure: an adult doing light 
activity needs around 1,500 calories per day to maintain basic function, though they will 
feel hungry.  
A child needs less depending on age. 1,200 calories per day is uncomfortable but 
survivable for a healthy adult over weeks. Below 1,000 calories per day you are in territory 
where cognitive function begins to degrade noticeably and physical capacity diminishes. 
Divide your total calorie count by the number of people in your household. That gives you 
the number of days you can sustain everyone at a given daily intake. Then decide: what 
daily intake are you targeting, and how many days does that buy you? 
This number is the most important strategic fact you have. It governs everything else: 
whether you try to trade for more food, whether you attempt to move, how urgently you 
need to find an alternative supply. 
The hierarchy of what to eat and when 
Not all food stores are equal. Some degrade quickly. Some are calorie -dense. Some 
provide nutrients that others lack. Eating in the wrong order wastes what you have. 
Eat in roughly this sequence: 
• Fresh food first, anything that will spoil within days regardless of whether you are 
rationing 
• Opened dry goods and partially used items before sealed ones 
• Lower calorie density items before higher ones, since you want to preserve your 
most calorie-dense stores for when need is greatest 
• Treat calorie-dense staples like cooking oil, rice, lentils, and dried beans as late -
stage reserves to be protected 
Cooking oil deserves special mention. It is the most calorie-dense common food item, at 
around 900 calories per 100ml, and it extends the caloric value of everything you cook it 
with.  
Protect your oil. Use it deliberately. A small amount of oil added to an otherwise thin meal 
significantly increases its caloric value.

A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
41 
Stretching staples further than you think possible 
When you are down to basics, the goal is maximum calories from minimum volume with 
minimum fuel use, since cooking fuel becomes its own scarce resource. 
Rice and grains.  Use more water than normal when cooking. It increases volume, 
extends the feeling of fullness, and reduces the amount of grain needed per meal. 
Congee, which is rice cooked with a very large amount of water into a thin porridge, uses 
a fraction of the ric e that normal cooking requires and can be flavored with almost 
anything. 
Legumes. Lentils and dried beans are among the most valuable foods in a shortage 
because they provide protein as well as calories. They require soaking and longer cooking 
times, which uses more fuel, so balance this against your fuel supply. Split lentils cook 
faster than whole ones and are worth prioritizing. 
Bread and flour. Flatbreads cooked on a dry pan use no oil and very little fuel. A small 
amount of flour produces a surprisingly filling result. If you have baking soda or yeast, you 
can produce slightly more volume, but neither is necessary. 
Bulking with water and vegetable matter.  Soups and broths extend solid food 
significantly. If you have any vegetables, even scraps or things past their best, cook them 
in water and use the liquid. Boiled greens, even ones you would not normally choose to 
eat, provide micronutrients that matter over weeks of restricted diet. 
The nutrients that become critical during extended 
shortage 
Calories keep you alive in the short term. Over weeks and months, specific nutrient 
deficiencies become a separate problem. 
Salt. Essential for basic bodily function. Easy to overlook because it is not a food in itself. 
Make sure your supply includes adequate salt and protect it. 
Vitamin C.  Scurvy becomes a real risk during extended food shortage. Any source of 
vitamin C matters: dried rosehips if you can find them, any preserved citrus, even pine 
needle tea which sounds unusual but is an effective source.  
If you are able to grow anything, fast -growing greens like cress provide vitamin C within 
days of sprouting. 
Protein. Without adequate protein, muscle mass degrades and immune function drops. 
Legumes are your primary source when meat is unavailable. Eggs, if you have access to 
chickens, are exceptionally valuable. Any source of protein should be prioritized.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
42 
Fat. Beyond its caloric density, fat is necessary for absorbing certain vitamins and for 
sustained cognitive function. Protect your oil stores. If you have access to any nuts or 
seeds, they are valuable for this reason. 
Managing children during food shortage 
Children during a food shortage require specific attention for two reasons. First, their 
caloric and nutritional needs relative to their body size are high, and deficiencies affect 
development in ways that matter beyond the immediate crisis.  
Second, they do not have the cognitive capacity to understand why they are hungry, 
which makes the psychological management of mealtimes both more important and 
more difficult. 
Some things that helped in our household and in families we knew: 
• Maintain the appearance of normalcy at mealtimes as much as possible. 
Presentation matters. A small amount of food served on a plate at a table, with 
whatever ritual your family normally has, is received differently than the same food 
handed over without ceremony. 
• Children handle hunger better when they are occupied and moving rather than 
sitting and thinking about it. Keep them active, keep them engaged, keep their 
minds elsewhere. 
• If you have to give unequal portions, and sometimes you will because a nursing 
mother or a sick person has greater immediate need, do not do it visibly at the 
table. Manage it in the kitchen. 
• Prioritize children's protein and fat intake even when reducing overall calories. The 
long-term cost of protein deficiency in a growing child is higher than in an adult. 
The point where you have to make harder decisions 
There is a level of shortage where normal rationing is no longer sufficient and the 
decisions become genuinely painful. When you are calculating days in single digits rather 
than weeks.  
When people in the household are showing signs of significant physical deterioration. 
At that point the question is no longer how to stretch what you have. It is how to get more. 
That means trading assets you have been reluctant to trade.  
It means attempting movement you have been reluctant to attempt. It means calling in 
relationships and obligations you have been holding in reserve.

A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
43 
Do not wait until you are at zero before making those moves. Make them when you have 
enough left to negotiate from, not when you are desperate.  
Desperation is visible and it costs you in every transaction it touches. 
The time to act is when you can see the bottom, not when you have reached it.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
44 
Chapter 10: What Happens When Medical 
Care Disappears 
The hospital in our neighborhood closed in the fourteenth month. Not all at once. It 
degraded first, staff leaving, supplies running out, the building itself becoming a target 
and then partially destroyed.  
By the time it stopped functioning as a hospital in any meaningful sense, most people 
had already stopped relying on it. You adapt before you realize you are adapting. 
What replaced it was a patchwork. People with any medical background at all became 
essential resources. Information about treatment spread through networks the way food 
and fuel information did.  
Households accumulated whatever medical supplies they could find and guarded them 
carefully. And people learned, out of necessity, things they never expected to need to 
know. 
This chapter covers the basics of that knowledge. It is not a substitute for proper medical 
training. If you can access any formal first aid course before or during a crisis, do it. But if 
you cannot, what follows will help you manage the situations most l ikely to arise, and 
help you understand the difference between what you can handle and what requires 
more than you have. 
The most important principle: prevent before you treat 
In a functioning medical system, treatment is the focus because prevention is already 
handled. Vaccines exist. Sanitation infrastructure works. Infected wounds get antibiotics 
before they become serious. 
When that system is gone, prevention becomes the most valuable medical activity you 
can engage in. 
Wound hygiene. The majority of war -related deaths that happen outside of immediate 
trauma are caused by infection, not by the initial injury. A wound that would be trivially 
treated with antibiotics in a hospital becomes life-threatening when those antibiotics do 
not exist.  
Clean every wound immediately and thoroughly. Use clean water, as much of it as you 
have. Remove visible debris. Cover the wound to keep it clean. Check it daily for signs of 
infection.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
45 
Sanitation. When municipal water and sewage stop working, waterborne illness 
becomes one of the leading causes of death, particularly among children. Boil drinking 
water or use purification tablets.  
Establish a latrine away from water sources and away from food preparation areas. Wash 
hands before handling food. These are simple measures with significant impact. 
Dental hygiene. This sounds minor until you are living through month six of a conflict with 
a dental abscess and no dentist.  
Dental infections can become systemic infections and they are extraordinarily painful 
and debilitating. Protect teeth by maintaining cleaning habits even when supplies are 
limited. Salt water rinses help when toothpaste runs out. 
Pest control. Rats, flies, and mosquitoes carry disease. In a collapsed infrastructure 
environment they multiply. Keep food sealed and stored off the ground. Eliminate 
standing water where mosquitoes breed. Patch holes in walls and windows where 
possible. 
Building a medical kit from available resources 
Before supplies disappear entirely from shops and markets, prioritize acquiring the 
following. In order of importance: 
Wound care: 
• Antiseptic solution, iodine or chlorhexidine preferred 
• Clean bandages and gauze in volume, you will use more than you expect 
• Medical tape or its substitute 
• Needles and thread for suturing, and the knowledge of when suturing is and is not 
appropriate 
• Tweezers for debris removal 
• Disposable gloves, as many as you can get 
Medication: 
• Broad spectrum antibiotics, amoxicillin covers a wide range of infections and is 
worth prioritizing 
• Oral rehydration salts, or the knowledge to make them from water, salt, and sugar 
• Paracetamol and ibuprofen in volume, for pain, fever, and inflammation 
• Antihistamines 
• Any prescription medication your household members depend on, stockpiled as 
far ahead as possible 
• Antidiarrheal medication

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
45 
Sanitation. When municipal water and sewage stop working, waterborne illness 
becomes one of the leading causes of death, particularly among children. Boil drinking 
water or use purification tablets.  
Establish a latrine away from water sources and away from food preparation areas. Wash 
hands before handling food. These are simple measures with significant impact. 
Dental hygiene. This sounds minor until you are living through month six of a conflict with 
a dental abscess and no dentist.  
Dental infections can become systemic infections and they are extraordinarily painful 
and debilitating. Protect teeth by maintaining cleaning habits even when supplies are 
limited. Salt water rinses help when toothpaste runs out. 
Pest control. Rats, flies, and mosquitoes carry disease. In a collapsed infrastructure 
environment they multiply. Keep food sealed and stored off the ground. Eliminate 
standing water where mosquitoes breed. Patch holes in walls and windows where 
possible. 
Building a medical kit from available resources 
Before supplies disappear entirely from shops and markets, prioritize acquiring the 
following. In order of importance: 
Wound care: 
• Antiseptic solution, iodine or chlorhexidine preferred 
• Clean bandages and gauze in volume, you will use more than you expect 
• Medical tape or its substitute 
• Needles and thread for suturing, and the knowledge of when suturing is and is not 
appropriate 
• Tweezers for debris removal 
• Disposable gloves, as many as you can get 
Medication: 
• Broad spectrum antibiotics, amoxicillin covers a wide range of infections and is 
worth prioritizing 
• Oral rehydration salts, or the knowledge to make them from water, salt, and sugar 
• Paracetamol and ibuprofen in volume, for pain, fever, and inflammation 
• Antihistamines 
• Any prescription medication your household members depend on, stockpiled as 
far ahead as possible 
• Antidiarrheal medication

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
46 
Other: 
• Thermometer 
• Blood pressure cuff if anyone in your household has cardiovascular conditions 
• Splinting materials, rigid and padded 
• A tourniquet, and the knowledge of how to use one correctly 
Treating the injuries most likely to occur 
Bleeding wounds 
The immediate priority with any bleeding wound is to stop the bleeding. Apply direct 
pressure with the cleanest material available and hold it. Do not remove the dressing to 
check if it is working. Add more material on top if bleeding soaks through. Hold pressure 
for longer than feels necessary, at minimum ten minutes without releasing. 
For limb wounds where direct pressure is not controlling severe bleeding, a tourniquet 
may be necessary. Apply it several inches above the wound, tight enough to stop the 
bleeding, and note the time it was applied. A tourniquet left on too long causes tiss ue 
damage, but uncontrolled bleeding kills faster. If a tourniquet is necessary, it was the right 
decision. 
Once bleeding is controlled, clean the wound thoroughly with clean water. If you have 
antiseptic, use it. Cover with a clean dressing. Monitor for infection daily. 
Signs of infection to watch for: 
• Increasing redness spreading outward from the wound 
• Warmth and swelling around the wound site 
• Pus or discharge that is cloudy or has an odor 
• Fever 
• Red streaking moving away from the wound, this is a serious sign requiring 
aggressive treatment immediately 
Fractures 
If a bone is broken, the goals are immobilization, pain management, and preventing 
further injury. You are almost certainly not going to set a complex fracture without 
training. What you can do is stabilize it. 
Splint the limb in the position you find it, not in a corrected position, using whatever rigid 
material is available padded with cloth to protect the skin. The splint should extend past 
the joints above and below the fracture.  
Check circulation below the splint regularly, press a fingernail until it goes white and see 
how quickly color returns. If circulation seems compromised, loosen the splint.
