source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
47 
Elevation reduces swelling. Pain management with ibuprofen helps with both pain and 
inflammation. Rest the limb and the person as much as the situation allows. 
Burns 
Cool the burn immediately with cool, not cold, water for at least ten minutes. Do not use 
ice, do not apply butter, oil, or toothpaste, and do not break blisters. Cover with a clean 
non-stick dressing if available. A clean plastic bag over a hand or foot b urn keeps it 
protected and moist. 
Serious burns covering large body areas, burns to the face, hands, feet, or genitals, or 
burns with charring or insensitivity are beyond field treatment and require professional 
care if any can be accessed. 
Respiratory problems from smoke and dust 
Bombing and fire create air quality conditions that cause serious respiratory distress. 
Keep people, particularly children and the elderly, away from smoke and dust. Wet cloth 
over the nose and mouth provides minimal but some filtration. Position people wi th 
respiratory distress sitting upright rather than lying down. 
Diarrhea and dehydration 
Diarrhea in a compromised sanitation environment is common and can kill quickly 
through dehydration, particularly in children. The treatment is aggressive oral 
rehydration. Oral rehydration solution is one liter of clean water, half a teaspoon of salt, 
and six teaspoons of sugar. Give it continuously in small amounts. A child who cannot 
keep fluids down requires urgent attention. 
When you are out of antibiotics 
Antibiotics are finite. There will come a point where you have used what you have and 
cannot replace them. 
When that happens, wound management becomes even more critical because you no 
longer have a fallback. Clean wounds with more water and more thoroughness than feels 
necessary.  
Honey, real honey, has genuine antibacterial properties and has been used on wounds 
effectively for centuries. Sugar directly applied to a wound also has some antibacterial 
effect by drawing moisture out of the wound environment. These are not equivalents of 
antibiotics but they are not nothing. 
Garlic has demonstrated antimicrobial properties in research settings. Crushed garlic 
applied to a wound or consumed in significant quantity is not a substitute for medical 
treatment but in a situation with no alternatives it is worth knowing.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
47 
Elevation reduces swelling. Pain management with ibuprofen helps with both pain and 
inflammation. Rest the limb and the person as much as the situation allows. 
Burns 
Cool the burn immediately with cool, not cold, water for at least ten minutes. Do not use 
ice, do not apply butter, oil, or toothpaste, and do not break blisters. Cover with a clean 
non-stick dressing if available. A clean plastic bag over a hand or foot b urn keeps it 
protected and moist. 
Serious burns covering large body areas, burns to the face, hands, feet, or genitals, or 
burns with charring or insensitivity are beyond field treatment and require professional 
care if any can be accessed. 
Respiratory problems from smoke and dust 
Bombing and fire create air quality conditions that cause serious respiratory distress. 
Keep people, particularly children and the elderly, away from smoke and dust. Wet cloth 
over the nose and mouth provides minimal but some filtration. Position people wi th 
respiratory distress sitting upright rather than lying down. 
Diarrhea and dehydration 
Diarrhea in a compromised sanitation environment is common and can kill quickly 
through dehydration, particularly in children. The treatment is aggressive oral 
rehydration. Oral rehydration solution is one liter of clean water, half a teaspoon of salt, 
and six teaspoons of sugar. Give it continuously in small amounts. A child who cannot 
keep fluids down requires urgent attention. 
When you are out of antibiotics 
Antibiotics are finite. There will come a point where you have used what you have and 
cannot replace them. 
When that happens, wound management becomes even more critical because you no 
longer have a fallback. Clean wounds with more water and more thoroughness than feels 
necessary.  
Honey, real honey, has genuine antibacterial properties and has been used on wounds 
effectively for centuries. Sugar directly applied to a wound also has some antibacterial 
effect by drawing moisture out of the wound environment. These are not equivalents of 
antibiotics but they are not nothing. 
Garlic has demonstrated antimicrobial properties in research settings. Crushed garlic 
applied to a wound or consumed in significant quantity is not a substitute for medical 
treatment but in a situation with no alternatives it is worth knowing.

Diarrhea in a compromised sanitation environment is common and can kill quickly 
through dehydration, particularly in children. The treatment is aggressive oral 
rehydration. Oral rehydration solution is one liter of clean water, half a teaspoon of salt, 
and six teaspoons of sugar. Give it continuously in small amounts. A child who cannot 
keep fluids down requires urgent attention. 
When you are out of antibiotics 
Antibiotics are finite. There will come a point where you have used what you have and 
cannot replace them. 
When that happens, wound management becomes even more critical because you no 
longer have a fallback. Clean wounds with more water and more thoroughness than feels 
necessary.  
Honey, real honey, has genuine antibacterial properties and has been used on wounds 
effectively for centuries. Sugar directly applied to a wound also has some antibacterial 
effect by drawing moisture out of the wound environment. These are not equivalents of 
antibiotics but they are not nothing. 
Garlic has demonstrated antimicrobial properties in research settings. Crushed garlic 
applied to a wound or consumed in significant quantity is not a substitute for medical 
treatment but in a situation with no alternatives it is worth knowing.

A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
47 
Elevation reduces swelling. Pain management with ibuprofen helps with both pain and 
inflammation. Rest the limb and the person as much as the situation allows. 
Burns 
Cool the burn immediately with cool, not cold, water for at least ten minutes. Do not use 
ice, do not apply butter, oil, or toothpaste, and do not break blisters. Cover with a clean 
non-stick dressing if available. A clean plastic bag over a hand or foot b urn keeps it 
protected and moist. 
Serious burns covering large body areas, burns to the face, hands, feet, or genitals, or 
burns with charring or insensitivity are beyond field treatment and require professional 
care if any can be accessed. 
Respiratory problems from smoke and dust 
Bombing and fire create air quality conditions that cause serious respiratory distress. 
Keep people, particularly children and the elderly, away from smoke and dust. Wet cloth 
over the nose and mouth provides minimal but some filtration. Position people wi th 
respiratory distress sitting upright rather than lying down.
